## Solution

**Answer: Yes.** For every infinite set $X$, there exists a surjective two-to-one function $f: X \to X$.

### Proof

We use a standard fact of cardinal arithmetic (a theorem of ZFC):

> **Fact.** For every infinite set $X$, there is a bijection $X \times \{0,1\} \to X$; equivalently $|X| = 2|X|$.

*Brief justification of the Fact.* Let $\kappa = |X|$ be an infinite cardinal. By the well-ordering theorem, $X$ can be well-ordered, so we may identify $X$ with the initial ordinal $\kappa$. The canonical (Gödel) well-ordering of $\kappa \times \kappa$ has order type $\kappa$, giving a bijection $\kappa \times \kappa \to \kappa$; hence $|\kappa \times \kappa| = \kappa$, i.e. $\kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa$. Since $\kappa \le 2\kappa \le \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa$, we obtain $2\kappa = \kappa$. Thus $|X \times \{0,1\}| = 2|X| = |X|$, yielding a bijection $\varphi: X \times \{0,1\} \to X$. $\square$

**Construction.** Fix a bijection $\varphi: X \times \{0,1\} \to X$ (which exists by the Fact, since $X$ is infinite). Define $f: X \to X$ by

$$f\big(\varphi(x, i)\big) = x \qquad \text{for all } (x, i) \in X \times \{0,1\}.$$

Since $\varphi$ is a bijection, every element of $X$ is *uniquely* of the form $\varphi(x,i)$ for some $(x,i) \in X\times\{0,1\}$, so $f$ is well-defined on all of $X$.

**$f$ is surjective.** For any $y \in X$, we have $y = f(\varphi(y, 0))$, so $y$ lies in the image of $f$.

**$f$ is two-to-one.** For any $y \in X$, a point $z \in X$ satisfies $f(z) = y$ iff $z = \varphi(y, i)$ for some $i \in \{0,1\}$. Hence

$$f^{-1}(\{y\}) = \{\,\varphi(y,0),\ \varphi(y,1)\,\}.$$

These two elements are distinct because $\varphi$ is injective and $(y,0) \neq (y,1)$. Therefore every fiber has exactly two elements.

We have produced a surjective, two-to-one function $f: X \to X$ for an arbitrary infinite set $X$. $\blacksquare$
